Executive Summary Sodium Metal Production for Indian Pharma
Executive Summary
India's pharmaceutical sodium supply is dominated by a single source country — three variables determine whether greenfield domestic production is viable
This analysis supports a go/no-go decision on greenfield pharmaceutical-grade sodium production in India, and identifies the three variables that determine investment viability.
Finding 1 — Supply concentration risk is acute
India sources approximately 75% of its pharmaceutical-grade sodium from China. At 7,500 tonnes per year, even a moderate tariff event (15%+) would push spot prices from USD 2.67/kg to above USD 4.20/kg — eliminating margin for most finished goods manufacturers. There is no domestic supplier capable of substituting this volume within a 24-month horizon.
75%
China's share of India's pharma sodium imports
Finding 2 — Domestic production economics are marginal at small scale
Below 6,000 tonnes annual output, no modelled scenario produces an IRR that exceeds cost of capital. The minimum viable greenfield requires approximately INR 280 crore in capital expenditure. This is not a market where incremental entry is rational.
INR
280Cr
estimated minimum viable greenfield capex
Finding 3 — Regulatory timeline is the critical path risk
Greenfield approval under current CDSCO and state environmental frameworks adds 18–24 months before commissioning. Any capital deployment decision must account for this lead time before the first tonne is produced.
18–24
months
CDSCO + state environmental approval timeline
Finding 4 — The market is not contestable at current pricing
At USD 2.67/kg, China-origin supply undercuts the production cost of any greenfield Indian facility at volumes below 8,000 tonnes/year. Entry is viable only if: (a) China import costs rise materially, (b) a captive supply rationale exists independent of market pricing, or (c) the investment horizon exceeds 7 years.

The data narrows the decision to two variables: scale and timing. The sections that follow provide the evidence base for both.

India: 75% import dependency on a single source Sodium Metal Production for Indian Pharma
1.1
China supplies 7,500 tonnes annually; no other source exceeds 8% market share
India imports approximately 7,500 tonnes of pharmaceutical-grade sodium annually.1 China supplies 75% of this volume.

No domestic producer holds WHO-GMP certification for pharmaceutical-grade sodium.2 This is a single-source dependency with a 14–18 week supply chain — and no credible domestic substitute within a 24-month horizon. Three Chinese producers — Inner Mongolia Lantai, Tianjin Zibo, and Wuxi Yinda — account for the majority of certified supply reaching Indian pharmaceutical manufacturers.3

Import prices have held below USD 3.00/kg for five consecutive years, driven by structural overcapacity in Chinese chlor-alkali production.4 The 2024 average CIF import price stands at USD 2.67/kg — a level that undercuts the production cost of any new greenfield Indian facility at volumes below 8,000 tonnes per year. This means any domestic production decision is not currently justified on price alone; the investment thesis depends on supply security value, not cost arbitrage.

Japan (6%), South Korea (4%), and Germany (3%) supply the remainder. No single alternative source exceeds 8% market share.5 In a supply disruption scenario — whether tariff-driven or logistic — Indian manufacturers face an 8–12 week re-sourcing window before production impact. No stockpiling protocol currently exists at the sector level.

1.2
Import prices have held below USD 3.00/kg for five consecutive years — Chinese overcapacity is the mechanism
The 2024 average CIF price of USD 2.67/kg represents the floor of a sustained compression cycle driven by Chinese chlor-alkali overcapacity.4

Between 2020 and 2024, the China-origin price declined 11% in nominal terms while landed costs for European and Korean alternatives remained 25–55% above Chinese parity. This price differential explains the consolidation of Indian pharmaceutical buyers onto Chinese supply chains — and makes domestic production economics structurally challenging at current import prices.

Source: DGCI&S Annual Import Data, 2020–2024. Ministry of Commerce and Industry, India. Caspr analysis.

The 5-year CAGR in Chinese import volume of 4.2% exceeds overall market growth of 2.4% — confirming that market share consolidation onto Chinese supply is structural, not cyclical. At the 2024 price of USD 2.67/kg, Chinese supply undercuts the production cost threshold of any new Indian greenfield facility at all modelled scales below 8,000 tonnes per year.

A 15% import tariff — the scenario modelled in Section 11 — would bring the effective landed price to USD 3.07/kg, still below the greenfield break-even at 6,000 tonnes (INR 212/kg at current INR/USD). A 25% tariff would cross the break-even threshold at approximately 6,400 tonnes annual scale.

Base-case IRR 22% — contingent on scale and premium Sodium Metal Production for Indian Pharma
14.2 — 14.3
EBITDA turns positive at 5,200 tonnes; IRR is viable in 7 of 9 modelled scenarios
The financial model spans three scenarios across three production volumes — nine combinations in total.8 Base case assumptions: 8% domestic price premium to China CIF, INR 280 crore capex, 85% capacity utilisation from year 2.

EBITDA margin stabilises at 18–22% above 6,000 tonnes. Below 5,200 tonnes in any scenario, EBITDA is negative. This means the facility cannot service debt or generate returns at small scale — scale is the primary value driver.

IRR sensitivity across the same nine scenarios confirms the investment is viable (IRR >15%) in 7 of 9 combinations. The two exceptions are: (1) downside price at 4,000 tonnes, and (2) downside price at 5,000 tonnes.

1.2 — Supplementary
China's share of India's pharmaceutical sodium imports has grown from 70% to 75% over four years — consolidation is accelerating
Import volume grew at 2.4% CAGR 2020–2024; China's share increased 5 percentage points over the same period, confirming structural consolidation onto Chinese supply.
Figure 1.1 — India pharmaceutical-grade sodium imports by source country (tonnes/year), 2020–2024
Source: DGCI&S Annual Import Data, 2020–2024. Ministry of Commerce and Industry, India. Caspr analysis.

The chart confirms what the price data implies: Chinese supply is not merely dominant — it is growing as a share of total imports while every alternative source stagnates or declines. At 75% in 2024, one percentage point of annual share gain brings the dependency to 80% by 2029 on the current trend. This means the supply security risk worsens with time absent a deliberate domestic production strategy.
